title: Simplify Responsibly
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that educational solutions are hopelessly complex and that this complexity is why teachers experience back-to-school meetings as a deluge of initiatives they cannot retain. The remedy he proposes is reduction: the best school leaders pare down mission statements, professional development plans and definitions of quality teaching until they can be held in one mind, and teachers must do the same for themselves. He applies a simple test, that if you cannot summarize a thing in a sentence you cannot expect it to be repeated or mastered. The qualifier in the title matters, though: simplified models must be tested hard against classroom reality, as he claims to have done with his five key beliefs and six things frameworks. The piece closes by endorsing the line often attributed to Einstein, as simple as possible but not simpler. This is a short, close call on length, but it makes a clear and quotable claim.
points: Teachers disengage from school improvement not from laziness but from lack of coherence, clarity and simplicity in the plans handed to them.
The leader's core task is reduction: if an initiative cannot be summarized in a sentence, staff cannot be expected to retain or master it.
Teachers share the work of simplification, since leaders are themselves too inundated to think clearly.
Simplification is only responsible if the simplified model is tested repeatedly against classroom practice.
quotes: At present, most teachers experience “back to school” meetings as the annual deluge of new plans and strategies and initiatives and goals and targets and procedures. For lack of a coherent sense of the whole, they despair or disengage or throw up their hands.
Chances are that if you can't summarize a thing in a sentence, you can't easily repeat it, and so you can't expect that your overwhelmed teachers will somehow magically retain and master it.

The work of the leader, then, is reduction and simplification. And, since some leaders are not so good at this — after all, they are even more inundated with expectations and pressures and policies and parent calls than teachers are, and so it is very hard for leaders to think clearly — that's the work of the teacher, too.

Here's the thing: simplification has to be done carefully. We need to create simplified models of what the work is — so take the five key beliefs I write about, or the “six things” in my latest book — and then test them intensely.
Allegedly, Einstein said, “Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler.
